who: People who cannot rotate a device
Low vision users who prefer landscape
Anyone with a phone on a stand
takeaways: Do not lock content to portrait or landscape. It works in both, unless one orientation is essential.
Some people have a device fixed in one position, on a wheelchair or a bed mount, and cannot turn it.
The layout can adapt to each orientation. It does not have to look the same in both.
Essential means the task cannot work otherwise, such as a piano keyboard app or photographing a bank check.
failures: A “Rotate your device” screen that blocks the app
A landscape-only video player with no portrait view
check: Design key screens in both portrait and landscape frames.
Turn the prototype or build on a real device and complete a task each way.
For any locked screen, write down why that orientation is essential.

quiz.question: A video app’s player looks best in landscape. What should happen when a phone is held upright?
options: Play in portrait, in a smaller frame
quiz.why: Landscape is nicer for video, but not essential. Someone with a mounted phone still needs to watch, so the player adapts instead of refusing.

spec: State that each screen supports both orientations.
Show how the layout changes between them.
Mark any screen locked to one orientation, with the essential reason.
review: What does this screen look like on its side?
Is this orientation lock essential, or just easier?
Can someone with a mounted device finish this flow?
tradeoff: Designing two orientations costs time, and a lock is tempting. Use responsive layouts that rearrange themselves, and save locks for the rare screen that truly needs one.
system: Define every template with portrait and landscape layouts, and make orientation locks an exception that needs a written reason.
pitch: Some customers cannot turn their phone. If our app only works one way up, they cannot use it at all.
